The energy absorbed by the inductor (Resistance neglected) in the first 2 sec, [latex]E_L=\int_{0}^{T}Li\frac{di}{dt}=E_{L_1}+E_{L_2} [/latex] [latex]E_{L_1}=\int_{0}^{2}Li \left (\frac{di}{dt} \right )dt [/latex] [latex]\;\;=\int_{0}^{2} 2 \times 3t \times 3\; dt [/latex] [latex]\;\;=18\int_{0}^{2}t\; dt [/latex] [latex]\;\;=18 \times \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{t^2}{2} \end{matrix}\right|^2_0 [/latex] [latex]\;\;= 18 \times \left [ \frac{4}{2}-0 \right ]=36J [/latex] The energy absorbed by the inductor in ([latex]2\rightarrow 4[/latex]) second [latex]E_{L_2}=\int_{2}^{4}Li\left ( \frac{di}{dt}dt \right ) [/latex] [latex]\;\;=\frac{2}{4}2 \times 6 \times 0 \;dt=0 J[/latex] A pure indictor does not dissipate enegy but only stores it. Due to resistance, some energy is dissipated in the resistor. Therefore, total energy stored in the inductor and the energy dissipated in the resistor. The energy dissipated by the resistance in 4 sec. [latex]E_R=\int_{0}^{T}i^2 R\;dt [/latex] [latex]\;\;=\int_{0}^{2}(3t)^2 \times 1 \;dt+\int_{2}^{4}6^2 \times 1 \; dt[/latex] [latex] \;\;=9\int_{0}^{2}t^2\;dt +36\int_{2}^{4}1 \; dt [/latex] [latex]\;\;=9 \times \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{t^3}{3} \end{matrix}\right|_0^2+36t|_2^4[/latex] [latex] \;\;=9 \times \left ( \frac{8}{3} \right )+36 \times 2 [/latex] [latex]\;\;=24+72=96J[/latex] The total energy absorbed by the inductor in 4 sec [latex] =96 J +36 J =132 J[/latex]
questions.explanation_html:
For [latex]0 \lt t \lt 2s[/latex] current varies linearly with time and given as [latex]i(t)=3t[/latex] and for [latex]2s \lt t \lt 4s[/latex] current is constant, [latex]i(t)=6A[/latex].
The energy absorbed by the inductor (Resistance neglected) in the first 2 sec,
[latex]E_L=\int_{0}^{T}Li\frac{di}{dt}=E_{L_1}+E_{L_2} [/latex]

[latex]\;\;= 18 \times \left [ \frac{4}{2}-0 \right ]=36J [/latex]
The energy absorbed by the inductor in ([latex]2\rightarrow 4[/latex]) second
[latex]E_{L_2}=\int_{2}^{4}Li\left ( \frac{di}{dt}dt \right ) [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\frac{2}{4}2 \times 6 \times 0 \;dt=0 J[/latex]
A pure indictor does not dissipate enegy but only stores it. Due to resistance, some energy is dissipated in the resistor. Therefore, total energy stored in the inductor and the energy dissipated in the resistor.
The energy dissipated by the resistance in 4 sec.
[latex]E_R=\int_{0}^{T}i^2 R\;dt [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=\int_{0}^{2}(3t)^2 \times 1 \;dt+\int_{2}^{4}6^2 \times 1 \; dt[/latex]
[latex] \;\;=9\int_{0}^{2}t^2\;dt +36\int_{2}^{4}1 \; dt [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=9 \times \left.\begin{matrix} \frac{t^3}{3} \end{matrix}\right|_0^2+36t|_2^4[/latex]
[latex] \;\;=9 \times \left ( \frac{8}{3} \right )+36 \times 2 [/latex]
[latex]\;\;=24+72=96J[/latex]
The total energy absorbed by the inductor in 4 sec

[latex]I_P+I_Q+I_C+I_L=0[/latex]
[latex] 2+2+I_C+I_L=0 [/latex]
But, [latex]I_C=C \times \frac{dv}{dt} [/latex]

questions.question:
A stand alone engine driven synchronous generator is feeding a partly inductive
load. A capacitor is now connected across the load to completely nullify the
inductive current. For this operating condition.

options.A: the field current and fuel input have to be reduced
options.B: the field current and fuel input have to be increased
options.C: the field current has to be increased and fuel input left unaltered
options.D: the field current has to be reduced and fuel input left unaltered

questions.explanation: Assuming resistance of the armature to be zero. In first case, the generator is feeding a partly inductive load. It means that generator is supplying lagging power. The generator supplies a lagging power factor current when it is overexcited which is represented by [latex]E_{f_1}[/latex]. In second case, a capacitor is connected across the load to completely nullifythe inductive current. It means the generator supplies no reactive power and unity power factor current is drawn from the generator. The excitation ([latex]E_{f_2}[/latex]) corresponding to unity power factor is known as normal excitation. From the phasor diagram [latex]E_{f_1} \gt E_{f_2}[/latex] and as the field current approximately directly proportional to excitation, the field current has to be reduced. From phasor diagram [latex]E_{f_1} \sin \delta _1=E_{f_2} \sin \delta _2=\text{constant}[/latex] [latex]P_e(\text{ power delivered})=\frac{E_fV_t}{X_s}\sin \delta[/latex] Fuel input remains unaltered.
questions.explanation_html:
Assuming resistance of the armature to be zero. In first case, the generator is feeding a partly inductive load. It means that generator is supplying lagging power. The generator supplies a lagging power factor current when it is overexcited which is represented by [latex]E_{f_1}[/latex].
In second case, a capacitor is connected across the load to completely nullifythe inductive current. It means the generator supplies no reactive power and unity power factor current is drawn from the generator. The excitation ([latex]E_{f_2}[/latex]) corresponding to unity power factor is known as normal excitation.

From the phasor diagram [latex]E_{f_1} \gt E_{f_2}[/latex] and as the field current approximately directly proportional to excitation, the field current has to be reduced. From phasor diagram [latex]E_{f_1} \sin \delta _1=E_{f_2} \sin \delta _2=\text{constant}[/latex]
